991.event_title: King Christian X keeps up his rides through occupied Copenhagen
991.event: King Christian X of Denmark had long been in the habit of riding on horseback through the streets of Copenhagen, and after Germany occupied Denmark in April 1940 he continued the rides. Britannica notes that he rode frequently through the city during the occupation, showing that he had not given up his claim to national sovereignty. The Royal Danish Collection records that these rides created his image as the equestrian king and that many Danes still remember him riding among them during the occupation.
991.explanation: By remaining visible and within reach of ordinary citizens in a frightening time, the king became a focus of national loyalty and affection.
991.tie_back: The kural says courtesy comes easily to one who is easy for anyone to approach, and Christian X's accessible presence on the streets won him the lasting regard of his people.
991._accuracy_note: A reasonable illustration of approachability winning affection, though the rides were chiefly a symbol of sovereignty under occupation, and the episode appears elsewhere in the book.

992.event_title: Princess Diana shakes hands with an AIDS patient
992.event: In April 1987 Diana, Princess of Wales, opened Britain's first hospital ward dedicated to patients with HIV/AIDS, at the Middlesex Hospital in London. In front of the press she shook the hand of a patient without wearing gloves, at a time when many people wrongly believed the virus could be passed on by touch. The photograph circulated around the world and is credited with helping to challenge the stigma attached to the disease.
992.explanation: A member of the royal family used her position to show simple warmth to people who were being shunned.
992.tie_back: The kural says courtesy is made of loving kindness joined to birth in a worthy family, and Diana, born into an aristocratic family and married into the royal one, joined her rank to visible compassion.
992._accuracy_note: A good fit for the pairing of kindness and high birth; commentators read the kural's worthy family partly as a family of good conduct rather than rank alone, and the event appears elsewhere in the book.

993.event_title: Albert Einstein gives Marian Anderson a room when a hotel refuses her
993.event: After the African American contralto Marian Anderson sang at the McCarter Theatre in Princeton on 16 April 1937, the town's Nassau Inn refused her a room because of her race. Albert Einstein, who had attended the concert, invited her to stay at his home instead. The two became friends, and on later visits to Princeton she stayed with Einstein until his death in 1955.
993.explanation: Einstein saw in Anderson a kindred spirit and an artist he admired, and treated the colour line that the hotel enforced as meaningless.
993.tie_back: The kural says that real likeness between people lies in shared qualities of character rather than in bodily sameness, and the friendship between the physicist and the singer rested on exactly such kinship.
993._accuracy_note: A good illustration of likeness in character outweighing physical difference, though the sources document the hospitality and friendship more than their shared qualities as such.

994.event_title: Wangari Maathai receives the Nobel Peace Prize
994.place: Oslo, Norway, for work in Kenya
994.event: Wangari Maathai founded the Green Belt Movement in Kenya in 1977, organising women to plant tens of millions of trees while campaigning against deforestation, poverty and abuses of power. On 8 October 2004 the Norwegian Nobel Committee awarded her the Nobel Peace Prize for her contribution to sustainable development, democracy and peace. She was the first African woman to receive the prize.
994.explanation: Maathai's honour came from work that combined practical benefit to ordinary people with a stubborn defence of fairness and good government.
994.tie_back: The kural says the world praises the character of those who are useful to others through love of justice and doing good, and the Nobel committee honoured Maathai for exactly that combination.
994._accuracy_note: A strong fit for worldwide praise earned by justice joined to beneficence; the kural's stress on courtesy of character is less directly shown.

995.event_title: Australian airmen bury the Red Baron with full military honours
995.event: Manfred von Richthofen, Germany's most famous fighter pilot, known as the Red Baron, was shot down and killed over the Somme on 21 April 1918. The next day men of No. 3 Squadron, Australian Flying Corps, buried him in the cemetery at Bertangles with full military honours: men of the squadron fired a volley over the grave, and wreaths sent by British squadrons were laid on it. The Australian War Memorial holds film and photographs of the funeral.
995.explanation: In the middle of a bitter war, his enemies chose to honour a fallen opponent rather than celebrate over him.
995.tie_back: The kural says that those who understand people keep their courtesy even toward enemies, and the Australian airmen showed respect to the enemy airman who had shot down so many of their comrades.
995._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of courtesy toward an enemy; the kural's first line, about mockery hurting even in jest, is reflected only in the absence of gloating.

996.event_title: Gander shelters the passengers of 38 diverted airliners
996.event: When United States airspace closed after the attacks of 11 September 2001, 38 airliners carrying roughly 6,600 passengers and crew were diverted to Gander, Newfoundland, a town of about 10,000 people. Schools, churches and halls were turned into shelters, residents took strangers into their own homes, and local businesses and volunteers supplied food, clothing and medicines for several days until flights resumed. The town was later formally thanked by the United States for its help.
996.explanation: Ordinary people's kindness to strangers held things together at a moment when the world seemed to be coming apart.
996.tie_back: The kural says the world keeps going because it rests on people of courteous character, and the people of Gander showed how much a frightened world depends on such people.
996._accuracy_note: A reasonable but partial fit: the event shows decent people sustaining others in a crisis, while the kural makes a broader claim about the whole world resting on them; the event also appears elsewhere in the book.

997.event_title: Fritz Haber, Nobel chemist, directs the first chlorine gas attack
997.event: The German chemist Fritz Haber developed a practical method of synthesising ammonia from nitrogen and hydrogen, the basis of modern nitrogen fertiliser, and received the 1918 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for it. During the First World War he also led Germany's development of poison gas and supervised its first large-scale use, the chlorine attack at Ypres on 22 April 1915. After the war he was widely criticised, and in some circles shunned, for his part in chemical warfare.
997.explanation: Haber's career shows that outstanding intellectual brilliance and humane judgement are different things, and that the first does not guarantee the second.
997.tie_back: The kural says that those without humane qualities are no better than trees even if their minds are as sharp as a file, and Haber's brilliance did not prevent him from turning science to the mass killing of soldiers.
997._accuracy_note: A reasonable but partial fit: Haber's gas work illustrates sharp intellect divorced from humane restraint, but he acted from patriotic conviction and his fertiliser work fed millions, so a verdict on his whole character is harsher than the evidence warrants.

998.event_title: Gandhi gives Jan Smuts a pair of sandals he made himself
998.event: In South Africa Mohandas Gandhi led years of nonviolent campaigns against laws enforced by the government in which Jan Smuts was a leading minister, and he was jailed several times. Before leaving South Africa in 1914 Gandhi gave Smuts a pair of sandals he had made with his own hands. Smuts kept them for many years, and in 1939, writing for Gandhi's seventieth birthday, he said he had worn them for many summers and did not feel worthy to stand in the shoes of so great a man.
998.explanation: Gandhi treated his chief political opponent with personal courtesy and kindness, and the opponent came to respond with respect.
998.tie_back: The kural says that failing in courtesy even toward those who are unfriendly and do us wrong is the lowest disgrace, and Gandhi kept his courtesy toward the minister whose government had imprisoned him.
998._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of courtesy toward an adversary; details such as where the sandals were made and whether Smuts later returned them vary between accounts, so only the agreed core is given. The episode also appears elsewhere in the book.

999.event_title: The Christmas Truce on the Western Front
999.place: Western Front, Belgium and northern France
999.event: Late on Christmas Eve 1914, British troops in parts of the Western Front heard German soldiers in the opposite trenches singing carols and saw lanterns and small trees along their parapets. On Christmas Day men from both sides walked out into no man's land, exchanged food, tobacco and souvenirs, took photographs, buried their dead and in places played impromptu football. The truces were unofficial and uneven, fighting continued elsewhere, and there was no comparable truce later in the war.
999.explanation: For a brief moment, sharing simple good cheer with the enemy lifted some of the darkness of the war for the men in the trenches.
999.tie_back: The kural says that for those unable to share friendly cheer the wide world is dark even in daylight, and the truce showed the reverse: shared cheer brought light into one of history's darkest settings.
999._accuracy_note: Next-best only: the event illustrates the kural by contrast rather than directly, and the truce also appears elsewhere in the book.

1000.event_title: Leona Helmsley is convicted of tax evasion
1000.event: The hotel and property billionaire Leona Helmsley was tried in federal court in New York in 1989, and many of the witnesses were her own former employees, whose testimony portrayed her as harsh and abusive toward staff. On 30 August 1989 she was convicted of evading about 1.2 million dollars in federal income tax by charging more than 4 million dollars of personal expenses, mostly renovations to her Connecticut estate, to her businesses. In December 1989 she was sentenced to four years in prison and heavy fines, and the press had long nicknamed her the Queen of Mean.
1000.explanation: Helmsley's great fortune brought her public contempt rather than honour, largely because of how she treated the people who worked for her.
1000.tie_back: The kural says that great wealth in the hands of someone without courtesy is like good milk spoiled by an unclean vessel, and Helmsley's wealth was soured in the public eye by her treatment of others.
1000._accuracy_note: A good fit for wealth spoiled by a lack of courtesy, though her conviction was for tax crimes rather than for her treatment of staff.
